title: DNS resolution from browser to server
description: Understand how domain names are resolved to IP addresses, from browser input to the final server connection, including recursive queries, caching, and common failure modes.

data.text: Every time you visit a website, your computer must translate a human-readable name like `example.com` into a machine-readable IP address like `93.184.216.34`. This translation is called **DNS resolution**, and it happens before your browser ever sends an HTTP request. Understanding this process is essential for diagnosing slow page loads, debugging regional outages, and configuring custom domains.

The Domain Name System (DNS) is often described as the phone book of the internet. Instead of memorizing numeric IP addresses, you type domain names. DNS maps those names to addresses so browsers can locate servers. Without DNS, you would need to know the exact IP of every service you use.

items: DNS turns domain names into IP addresses
It operates over UDP and TCP port 53
Results are cached at multiple layers to improve speed
A single domain can resolve to multiple IPs for load distribution

data.text: The resolution path step by step

data.title: Typical resolution flow
items: The browser checks its own DNS cache.
If not cached, the operating system checks its resolver cache.
The query is sent to the configured DNS resolver (often your ISP or a public resolver like 1.1.1.1).
If the resolver has the answer cached, it returns immediately.
If not, the resolver performs a recursive lookup: root servers, TLD servers, and finally authoritative servers.
The resolver returns the IP address, which is then cached at every layer.
The browser opens a TCP/TLS connection to that IP.

data.caption: How a browser resolves a domain to an IP address
data.mermaid:
graph TD
    A[Browser] --> B{Local cache?}
    B -->|yes| Z[Use cached IP]
    B -->|no| C[OS resolver cache]
    C -->|yes| Z
    C -->|no| D[Configured DNS resolver]
    D -->|cached| Z
    D -->|not cached| E[Root server]
    E --> F[TLD server]
    F --> G[Authoritative server]
    G --> H[Return IP]
    H --> I[Cache at resolver]
    I --> Z
    Z --> J[Connect to server]

data.title: Performance insight
data.text: Cached DNS results can skip the entire recursive chain. That is why clearing your DNS cache can temporarily slow down browsing.

items: Local or ISP cache serving stale records

data.title: Real-world clue
data.text: If `nslookup example.com` returns one IP but your browser still cannot load the site, the problem is likely downstream of DNS: TLS, routing, or the server itself.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: DNS resolution converts domain names to IP addresses before any HTTP traffic begins.
Caching at the browser, OS, and resolver levels dramatically affects speed.
Common record types include A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, and TXT.
DNS failures often masquerade as server outages.
data.takeaway: Mastering DNS gives you a systematic way to diagnose connection failures that look like server problems but originate in name resolution.

items.question: Why does a new domain take time to work?
items.answer: DNS changes need to propagate through caches worldwide. TTL values control how long old records are kept, so changes can take from minutes to hours to become visible everywhere.

items.question: What does 'propagation' really mean?
items.answer: It means recursive resolvers and local caches still hold the old record until their TTL expires. You cannot force every cache in the world to refresh immediately.

items.question: Should I use my ISP's DNS or a public resolver?
items.answer: Public resolvers like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8 are often faster, more private, and more reliable than ISP defaults. The best choice depends on your network environment and privacy requirements.

data.text: DNS is the first domino. If it falls, everything after it fails silently.
